sessions.title: Quick body scan
script: Three minutes, just for you. Wherever you are, in your chair or standing up, is perfectly fine.
Close your eyes if you'd like, or let your gaze rest low, on the desk or the floor in front of you.
Breathe in through your nose… and breathe out a little longer, like a quiet sigh.
[pause 3s]
We're going to do a quick tour of the body, the way you'd pat your pockets before heading out.
Start with your feet. Feel them against the floor, the weight in your heels.
Your toes can soften inside your shoes.
Your calves, your knees, your thighs. Let them be heavy, simply resting, as if your legs had nothing left to carry.
Move up to your hips. Feel how your pelvis sits on the chair, the weight settling there, the seat holding you up.
Then your lower back. If you're slumped, lift up just a little, without stiffening.
All along your back, let the chair, or your own spine, do the holding. You don't have to hold yourself up alone.
Now your belly. Is it pulled in, tight? You can let it go, let it be soft, rounding a little as you breathe in.
Your chest. Notice your breath lifting it, without trying to change anything. Just this movement, rising and falling.
[pause 3s]
Your shoulders. They often creep up without us noticing, especially in front of a screen.
Let them drop half an inch, and then a little more, as if someone had rested warm hands on them.
Your arms grow heavy, from your shoulders down to your elbows, from your elbows down to your wrists.
Your hands rest, your fingers uncurl. There's nothing you need to hold on to right now.
Your face. Your forehead can smooth out, the space between your eyebrows can widen. Your cheeks soften.
Your eyes can rest behind your eyelids. And your jaw… check whether your teeth are touching. Let a little space open between them, lips gently closed, tongue at ease.
And now your whole body, all at once, from your feet to the top of your head, one single presence, breathing.
Notice the spot that felt tightest a moment ago. Has it shifted at all? If not, that's okay. You noticed it, and that already counts for a lot.
Let's take one last breath together. Breathe in slowly through your nose, feeling your whole body…
[pause 3s]
And breathe out through your mouth, long and slow, letting go of whatever is ready to go.
Open your eyes if they were closed, or lift your gaze. Wiggle your fingers and toes, and roll your shoulders once.
You can come back to this little tour any time today, even for thirty seconds, between two emails.

sessions.title: Shoulders and jaw
script: Hello. If you're here, maybe something is pulling at the back of your neck, or you've just caught yourself clenching your teeth.
Sit down with your feet flat on the floor, your back upright but not rigid, your hands resting on your thighs.
For these next few minutes, stay within what feels comfortable. If a movement hurts, make it smaller, or simply imagine doing it.
Take an easy breath in through your nose… and let it flow slowly out, a little longer than it came in.
[pause 3s]
Do a quick check-in. Your shoulders, your neck, your jaw. Which of the three feels tightest today?
There's no right answer. Just notice where your attention goes first.
Let's begin with the shoulders. On your next breath in, lift them up toward your ears. Slowly, like a big, exaggerated shrug.
Keep them up there. Feel the effort in your upper back, along the sides of your neck.
And as you breathe out, let them drop all at once. Like setting down a bag that's far too heavy.
Feel the difference. The warmth, maybe a faint tingling, a sense of space opening up.
Once more. Breathe in, lifting… hold for a moment…
And let everything go as you blow the air out through your mouth.
A third time, at your own pace. Lift, hold, and release.
After this last release, let your shoulders find where they actually belong. A little lower, a little wider than before.
[pause 3s]
Now the neck. Let your head tilt slowly to the right, your ear drifting down toward your shoulder. The shoulder itself stays low.
Only go as far as a gentle stretch along the left side of your neck. No further.
Stay there for two breaths. With every exhale, the weight of your head does the work for you. Imagine your breath softening that side of your neck, from ear to collarbone.
Bring your head back to center, slowly, as if it were floating.
And now to the left. Your left ear lowers, and the right side of your neck lengthens.
Breathe into that stretch. There's nothing to force. Notice whether this side feels different, looser or stiffer.
Come back to center. Let your chin sink a little toward your chest. Feel the back of your neck lengthen, all the way down into your upper back.
Then lift your head, one vertebra at a time, until it rests upright and balanced.
[pause 3s]
Now the jaw. It's one of the strongest muscles in your body, and it often works in secret: in the car, in front of a screen, during the night.
Open your mouth wide, slowly, as wide as feels comfortable. As if you were about to yawn.
If a real yawn comes, let it come. That's excellent news.
Then close gently, without letting your teeth touch.
Do it once more. Open wide… feel your cheeks stretch just in front of your ears… and release.
Now rest the tip of your tongue on the roof of your mouth, just behind your top teeth. No pressing.
Your lips stay closed, but your teeth part. Just a small gap, barely enough room for a grain of rice.
This is your jaw's natural resting position. The one it forgets when you're under pressure.
Let that space stay there. Breathe through your nose, feeling cool air coming in, warmer air flowing out.
[pause 3s]
If you'd like, you can add a little massage. Place your fingertips on your temples and make small, very slow circles.
Then move your fingers down to just in front of your ears, on your cheeks. Clench your teeth lightly and you'll feel a muscle bulge there: that's the masseter.
Unclench, and massage that muscle in small circles with gentle pressure. If it feels tender, just stroke it lightly.
Keep going for a few breaths, at your own pace. Feel the warmth of your fingers sinking in, and the muscle softening a little under the pressure.
Let your hands come back to rest on your thighs.
Check in once more. Shoulders: low. Neck: long. Jaw: loose, tongue resting on the roof of your mouth.
Notice whether the spot you picked at the start has changed. A little, a lot, or not at all. Whatever you find is fine.
Here's a small idea for the rest of your day. Pick something you do often: opening a door, glancing at your phone, waiting for the kettle to boil.
Each time, simply ask yourself: am I clenching my teeth? And let that little space come back.
You can return to your day now, with your shoulders a little lighter.

sessions.title: Shake off stress
script: Sometimes, sitting still and breathing calmly is just not possible. Your body is too wound up, and it needs to move. So let's move.
Stand up, if you can. Feet hip-width apart, knees soft and slightly bent, arms hanging by your sides.

One rule for the whole session: stay within what's comfortable. No jumping, no jerky movements, never any pain. If your back or knees are sore, do all of this sitting down, shaking just your arms and shoulders. That works too.
Breathe in through your nose, and blow out through your mouth, fully.
[pause 3s]
Let's start with your hands. Let them hang, wrists loose, and shake them. As if your fingers were wet and there was no towel in sight.
Fingers completely relaxed, flapping about. You can go a little faster, or slower. Find what feels good.
Now let the movement travel up into your wrists, your forearms, then your elbows.
Your whole arms are shaking now, floppy as ropes. In front of you, out to the sides, down low. Change direction as you like.
Notice whether your shoulders want to join in. Let them. They can bounce, shrug, and drop.
[pause 3s]
Now the legs. Without leaving the floor, start bouncing gently on your heels. Your heels lift just slightly and drop, again and again.
It's a small, springy bounce that comes from the knees. Feel the vibration travel up through your calves, your thighs, into your hips.
If you like, lift one foot and shake that leg, as if you were shaking sand out of your shoe. Then the other leg. Hold on to a wall or a chair if you need some balance.
Come back onto both feet, and keep bouncing. Let your breath stay free, through your nose or your mouth, however it comes.
Now let your whole body get involved. Heels bouncing, arms shaking, shoulders moving, belly jiggling too.
Let your head follow along, without throwing it around. Just loose, carried by everything else.
And your jaw… let it hang. Mouth slightly open, cheeks soft and wobbling a little. It might feel a bit silly, and that's absolutely fine.
If a sound wants to come out, let it. A loud breath, an "ahhh", a grunt, a laugh. Nobody's grading you.
Your body has built up momentum to face a danger that isn't coming. You're simply giving it a way to spend that energy.
Keep going, at your own pace. Shake out whatever needs shaking. Your upper back, your hips, your hands again, wherever things feel stuck.
[pause 3s]
A few more seconds. Maybe put a little more energy into it, if that feels good. One last burst, as if you were shaking off the last crumbs of the day.
And now, start to slow down. No sudden stop. The movement gets smaller, slower.
Your arms swing gently. Your heels barely bounce. Like a merry-go-round coming to the end of its ride.
Your shoulders settle, your knees soften, your hands slow down little by little. Smaller still. Just a slight tremble in your hands, in your knees.
And then… still.
[pause 3s]
Stay standing, knees still a little bent, arms hanging. Close your eyes if you feel steady, otherwise rest your gaze on the floor in front of you.
Notice what's happening now. In your hands, maybe tingling, buzzing, a sense of aliveness under the skin.
Maybe warmth in your arms, in your face. Your heart beating a little faster, and beginning to slow. You might feel it in your chest, or in your fingertips.
There's nothing to do with these sensations. Just notice them, the way you'd watch bubbles rising to the surface.
Feel your feet flat on the floor. Your body's weight sinking into the ground, spread between your heels and the balls of your feet.
Let your breath settle. No need to control it. Just notice how it finds its way, on its own, back toward a calmer rhythm.
Breathe in through your nose… and let the out-breath last a little longer, like a wave drawing back from the shore.
[pause 3s]
Once more. Breathe in… and breathe out, slowly.
Notice the contrast between the commotion a moment ago and this calm. Your body found this calm all by itself, once that energy had somewhere to go.
Open your eyes if they were closed. Take a few steps, look around you.
Next time you feel wired, remember: you don't have to sit still to calm down. You can shake first, and then stop.

sessions.title: Belly breathing
script: When we're stressed, the breath tends to climb. It settles high in the chest, quick and shallow, shoulders lifting with every inhale.
Babies breathe with their bellies without even thinking about it. You already know how to breathe this way. We're simply going to find it again, step by step.
Lie down on your back, knees bent if that's more comfortable. Or sit upright, with your feet flat on the floor. Either way, loosen your belt or anything tight around your waist.
Close your eyes, or let your gaze rest on a fixed point.
[pause 3s]
Now place one hand flat on your upper chest, just below your collarbones. And the other hand on your belly, around your navel.
Your hands are going to be your witnesses. They don't push. They listen.
For now, don't change anything about your breathing. Let it be exactly as it is.
Watch your two hands. Which one moves more as you breathe in? The top one, on your chest? The bottom one, on your belly? Or both, a little?
There's no wrong answer. If it's mostly your chest moving, that's very common. It's often the sign of a busy day, or of a long-standing habit.
Take a few more breaths to really feel what's happening under each hand.
[pause 3s]
Now let's invite the belly to take part. Imagine a soft balloon just behind your navel.
On your next breath in, through your nose, let that balloon gently fill. Your lower hand rises. Your upper hand stays almost still.
This isn't an effort from your stomach muscles. It's closer to the opposite: you release your belly and let it round out to make room for the air.
Beneath your lungs sits a large dome-shaped muscle, the diaphragm. As it moves down, it gently nudges your belly forward. That's all that's happening.
Try again. Breathe in, and feel your lower hand rise, like a small boat lifted by a gentle wave.
Now the out-breath. This part, you don't have to do. Let the air flow out through your nose, or through slightly parted lips.
Your belly sinks back on its own, like a balloon deflating without being squeezed. Your lower hand gently lowers.
Breathe in, the belly fills. Breathe out, it settles back, with no help.
[pause 3s]
If your upper hand is still moving a lot, that's fine. It comes with practice. You can also try letting your shoulders get really heavy, as if they're melting into the floor or the back of the chair.
And if you feel dizzy or uncomfortable at any point, just go back to your natural breathing. The goal isn't to breathe more, or harder.
Now slow things down a little. Not by taking in more air, but by taking more time.
The in-breath becomes slow and smooth. And the out-breath can stretch out a bit longer still, like a peaceful sigh.
Breathe in for three or four seconds, and out for four to six. Only if it feels pleasant. Otherwise, keep your own rhythm.
Your belly rises only slightly more than before. You don't need big breaths. A small wave in the right place is better than a big, forced one.
Let's do a few rounds together. Breathe in through your nose… two… three… your belly rounds out under your hand.
And breathe out… two… three… four… your belly settles back, effortlessly, like a sheet drifting down onto a bed.
Again. Breathe in… the balloon fills from the bottom up, your chest stays quiet.
Breathe out… slowly… and notice that still moment at the end of the breath, before the next in-breath arrives on its own.
[pause 3s]
Keep going at this pace, following your lower hand. The belly rises… and falls. Nothing else to do.
If your mind has wandered off, to a to-do list or a conversation, that's normal. Notice it, and gently bring your attention back under your lower hand.
Feel the warmth of your hand on your belly. The fabric under your fingers. The movement lifting your palm, then letting it sink again.
Notice the sides of your waist, too. As you breathe in, they widen a little, like an accordion opening. As you breathe out, they draw back in.
Each out-breath can carry away a little of the tension in your belly. The muscles let go, and space opens up for the next in-breath.
Let your jaw unclench and your shoulders drop. The quieter your upper body, the more easily your breath finds its way down to your belly.
Many people find that this slow, low breathing helps them feel more settled. Just let yourself feel what it's doing for you, today.
[pause 3s]
Now let your hands rest wherever they'd like. By your sides, or on your thighs.
Your belly may keep breathing on its own, or your breath may drift a little higher again. Notice, without correcting.
Notice how you feel compared to when you started. Slower, heavier, calmer? Or about the same? Every session is practice, and your body is learning even when you don't feel a big difference.
Deepen your breath a little. Move your fingers, your feet. Open your eyes whenever the moment feels right for you.

For the rest of your day, here's a simple idea. Three or four times, at a red light, waiting for the train, or after hanging up the phone, place a hand on your belly. And ask yourself: where is my breath, right here, right now? Then let it drop back down, just a little.

sessions.title: Knotted stomach
script: A ball in the pit of your stomach. A knot that tightens, a belly that clenches before a meeting, an appointment, a difficult conversation.
Lots of people feel stress right here. If that's you today, you're in the right place.
Settle into a seat with your back supported, or lie down with your knees bent. Loosen anything tight around your waist, if you can.
Let your eyes close, or let your gaze rest softly downward. Take an easy breath, and let the out-breath linger a little.
[pause 3s]
First, rub your hands together. Palm against palm, quite quickly, like on a cold winter morning at the bus stop.
Feel the friction, the warmth building in your palms and fingers.
Keep going a little longer… and stop. Hold your hands slightly apart for a moment, and feel that warmth between them, like a small cushion of warm air.
Now rest both hands on your belly. One just above your navel, in the soft hollow below your ribs. The other just below. Or wherever feels right.
Feel the warmth of your palms passing through the fabric, reaching your skin.
Your hands aren't trying to fix anything. They're just there. Like a friendly hand resting on a shoulder.
[pause 3s]
Take a few natural breaths, without changing anything. Feel how your belly moves under your hands. Maybe a lot, maybe very little. Maybe it feels frozen, as if it were holding its breath.
All of this is normal. When we're tense, the belly often closes up to protect itself. It's an old reflex, one that has long helped the body get ready to act.
Now, with curiosity, go and meet the sensation. As if you were discovering it for the very first time.
Where exactly is it? Higher up, under your ribs? In the middle, around your navel? Lower down?
How big is it? A marble, a tennis ball, a clenched fist? Does it have clear edges, or is it more spread out, a little blurry?
Is it hard, or more heavy? Warm, cool? Does it pull, prickle, weigh down, flutter?
Does it stay still, or does it move, pulse, tighten and loosen?
You don't need precise words. Just observe it the way you'd watch a cloud: its shape, its color, its outline.
[pause 3s]

And what's around it? Look for a place in your belly, or in your back, that feels neutral, or even comfortable. There's often one, right next door. Notice that the unpleasant sensation doesn't take up all the room.
Maybe your lower back, resting against the chair or the floor. Maybe your hips, or the warmth of your hands themselves. Let your attention rest there for a moment, then gently come back to the knot.
If your attention drifts toward what's worrying you, toward the scenarios and the "what ifs", that's normal. Come back to the sensation itself, in your body, right now.
And now, breathe as if your breath could wrap itself around this sensation.
As you breathe in, imagine the air traveling down to it and surrounding it, gently, on every side. Without pushing it, without chasing it away.
As you breathe out, simply leave it there, surrounded by a little more space.
Breathe in… the air flows down and wraps around. Breathe out… it leaves a little room around it.
Once more. Breathe in slowly… like a soft cloth settling all around it. Breathe out… and the sensation floats in a little more space.
[pause 3s]
Keep going like this, at your own pace. If you feel any discomfort or dizziness, just return to your natural breath.
Let your belly swell just slightly under your hands, just enough to feel it taking part. Nothing more.
Now bring your attention to the muscles of your belly. The ones that tighten without your say-so, like an inner belt.
With each out-breath, invite those muscles to loosen by one notch. Not all at once. Just one notch.
Breathe out… the belly softens a little. Breathe out again… the belt loosens a tiny bit more.
Imagine the warmth of your hands slowly melting into those muscles, like butter on warm toast.
The upper belly, just below your breastbone, can soften. The sides, at your waist, can widen. The lower belly can become softer, heavier.
And behind you, your lower back can let go too. Your belly and back form a single cylinder: when one softens, the other often follows.
If the sensation is still there, that's completely fine. We're not trying to make it disappear. We're making room for it.
[pause 3s]
And now, a phrase to offer it, silently. You can repeat it with me, or just listen.
You're allowed to be here.
This ball, this knot, is your body trying to protect you, in its own way. It's reacting to something that matters to you.
You're allowed to be here. I'm here too, with you.
Notice what happens when you stop fighting it. Maybe it shifts a little, softens, moves somewhere else. Maybe not. Both are normal.
Stay a few more breaths like this, warm hands on your belly, breath coming and going beneath them.
Nothing to achieve. Just being here, with your belly, with kindness. The way you'd sit beside a worried friend, without trying to talk them out of anything.
[pause 3s]
Before we finish, let your hands stay where they are a moment longer. Don't take them away just yet.
Feel the contact, the light weight of your palms, the warmth that lingers. Like a thank-you to your body, which is doing its best.
Notice how your belly feels now. Maybe a little softer, calmer. Or not yet. You've offered it a moment of attention, and that already means a lot.
And if stomach pain is strong, frequent, or unusual for you, talk to a doctor. This practice isn't a substitute for medical advice.
When the moment feels right, let your hands slide gently to your sides. Take a slightly fuller breath. Move your fingers, your shoulders.
Open your eyes, and come back to the room around you.
Later today, if the knot comes back, you know what to do: rub your hands together, rest them on your belly, and tell it, silently, that it's allowed to be here.

sessions.title: Release your back
script: Hours in front of a screen, on the commute, on the sofa… Your back carries all of it, without ever complaining out loud. For the next few minutes, the floor is going to do the carrying instead.
For this practice, lie on your back on a mat, a folded blanket, or a rug. A firm floor works better than a soft bed.
Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor, about hip-width apart, toes pointing forward.
If your head tips back and your chin lifts toward the ceiling, slide a book or two under your head, so the back of your neck stays long.
Rest your hands on your belly, or let your arms lie on the floor slightly away from your body, palms however you like.

One note: this isn't a treatment session. If you have back pain, an injury, or any doubts, adapt the position, and feel free to ask a health professional for advice. And if lying down isn't possible for you, you can follow along sitting, with your back against a chair.
[pause 3s]
Let your eyes close, or simply look at the ceiling with a soft gaze.
Take a slightly fuller breath. And as you breathe out, let a sigh escape, like when you finally set your bags down.

This position is called constructive rest. Bending your knees lets your lower back settle more easily. There's nothing to hold. If your knees want to fall out to the sides, let them lean against each other, or bring your feet a little closer together.
Take your time finding the spot where your legs almost balance on their own. Your thighs can let go, your hips can soften. Your legs aren't doing any work at all.
[pause 3s]
Now bring your attention to the back of your body. Start by finding the points of contact. The places where your back actually touches the floor.
The back of your head, resting on the floor or the book. Both shoulder blades. Maybe the middle of your back. Your pelvis. The soles of your feet.
Notice too the places that don't touch. Often the hollow of your neck, or the curve of your lower back. There's nothing to fix. These curves are natural.

Just feel the contrast between what's resting and what's floating. The floor, maybe a little cool under your hands. The fabric of your clothes against your skin. The pressure, stronger in some places, lighter in others.
[pause 3s]
Now come all the way down to the base of your spine, to the sacrum. That's the flat, triangle-shaped bone at the back of your pelvis, just above your tailbone.
Feel how it rests on the floor. Imagine it getting heavy. A little heavier with every out-breath, like a warm stone resting in the sand.
You don't need to press. Just let the weight do its work. Maybe you can feel a slight warmth there, where your pelvis meets the floor.
And as your sacrum grows heavier, bring your attention to your lower back, around the kidneys.
Imagine this area widening. Spreading out to the right and to the left, like dough left to rest.

The muscles on either side of your spine can loosen, softening toward the floor. Maybe the curve of your lower back eases a little closer to the mat, without you pushing it. Or maybe not. Either is fine.
If you feel stiffness or discomfort, don't fight it. Breathe around it and let it be there.
[pause 3s]
Now we'll travel up the spine, one vertebra at a time, the way you'd climb a staircase very slowly.

The lumbar vertebrae, at waist level. Five broad, sturdy vertebrae that carry much of your weight all day long. Let your attention rest on each one in turn, without worrying about counting them exactly.
Then the middle of your back, behind your stomach. This is where your ribs attach to your spine. Maybe you can feel their slight movement with every breath.
Keep climbing, vertebra by vertebra, up to the space between your shoulder blades. Each vertebra can settle onto the floor, one after another, like pearls on a necklace being laid on a table.
Notice whether any part of your spine feels stiffer, or more present. Rest your attention there a little longer. Imagine that with every out-breath, a tiny bit of space opens between those vertebrae.
Then the base of your neck. Your neck, long, resting on its support. And the back of your skull, heavy, held. Your head weighs about as much as a bowling ball. For once, you don't have to hold it up.
[pause 3s]
Now come to your shoulder blades, those two large flat bones at the top of your back.
Imagine them spreading out across the floor. Sliding gently away from each other, outward, opening up space between them.
Your upper back widens. Your shoulders move away from your ears. Your arms grow heavy, almost draping from your shoulders down to the floor.
Feel your whole upper back as one wide surface, spread out and held by the floor.
Now we'll breathe into the back. We're used to feeling the breath at the front, in the chest or belly. But your lungs also fill the back of your ribcage.
On your next breath in, see if you can feel your back against the floor. Maybe it presses down just a touch more. Maybe your ribs spread slightly backward and out to the sides.
As you breathe out, your back settles again, a little heavier.
[pause 3s]
Breathe in, and feel your back widen against the floor. Breathe out, and let it give in completely.
Imagine your breath reaching into your lower back too, massaging it from the inside, ever so gently, with every breath.
Breathe in… your lower back opens a little, like a sponge filling with water. Breathe out… it rests, wider, heavier.
If your mind slips off toward your to-do list, that's normal. Come back to the contact with the floor. It's always there.
Stay like this for a few breaths, not looking for anything. The floor is holding you. You don't have to hold yourself up anymore.
[pause 3s]
Now take a moment to feel your back as a whole. From your sacrum to the back of your head. Wide, long, resting.
Compare it with the start of the session. Is your back touching the floor in new places? Does it feel wider, heavier, calmer? Just notice, without expecting anything.
[pause 3s]
It's time to come back, taking care of your back as you do. Start by moving your fingers and toes. Breathe a little more deeply.
Let your knees fall gently together to the right, or to whichever side suits you. And roll your whole body onto that side, all in one piece, like a log.
Stay lying on your side for a moment, your head resting on your arm. Take a breath or two here.
Then use your hands to push yourself up, pressing into the floor. Your head comes up last, without any rush.
Once you're sitting, pause for a moment. Feel your back lengthening upward, and see whether it keeps some of that width.
Throughout your day, every time you get up from your chair, you can recall this feeling. A wide, supported back that doesn't have to hold everything up on its own.

sessions.title: Progressive muscle relaxation
script: "Just relax." Easy to say. But if you feel like you don't really know how, this session is made for you.
The idea is simple: you tense a group of muscles for a few seconds, then let go. By feeling the tension, and then its absence, your body learns the difference.
Settle into a chair with your feet flat on the floor, or lie down on your back. Close your eyes if that's comfortable.
One important guideline for the whole session: tense to about fifty percent of your strength. Not all the way. Enough to clearly feel the muscle working, but never to the point of pain.
If an area is injured or sore, or if you get a cramp, simply skip that step and imagine the movement instead. And while you're tensing, keep breathing normally. Don't hold your breath.

Before we begin, do a quick check-in. Where do you feel tense, right here, right now? Your shoulders, your jaw, your belly, your hands? Just note it, without trying to change it. We'll come back to it at the end.
Take an easy breath in… and let it go.
[pause 3s]
We'll start with your hands and forearms. Make two fists. Squeeze gradually, to about half your strength.
Feel the tension in your fingers, in your palms, then climbing into your wrists and along the top of your forearms. Observe it. It's hard, warm, maybe trembling slightly.
Hold it… five… four… three… two… one…
And release. Open your hands, all at once. Let your fingers uncurl on their own, without stretching them out.
Notice what's happening in your hands now. Maybe tingling, warmth, heaviness. Your forearms softening.
That's the sensation we're here for: the letting go, right after the effort. Take your time to really savor it.
And compare your hands with the rest of your body, which hasn't done anything yet. Can you feel a difference? Even a slight one counts.
[pause 3s]
Now your arms and shoulders. Bend your elbows and press your arms against your ribs, tightening your upper arms, your biceps.
At the same time, lift your shoulders toward your ears. Your whole upper body draws in, like when you're cold at a bus stop.
Feel the tension in your arms, across the tops of your shoulders, at the base of your neck. Hold it. Breathe. Five… four… three… two… one…
And let go. Let your shoulders drop, your arms fall back onto your thighs or by your sides.
Feel your shoulders sink a little further, afterward. As if they were carrying on downward, all by themselves.
Your arms are heavy. Your shoulders are wide. And this area, which works nonstop all day, can finally settle. Each out-breath lets it sink just a hair lower.
[pause 3s]
Now your face, in three steps. First, your forehead. Raise your eyebrows as high as you can, as if you were very surprised. Feel your forehead wrinkle, the skin drawing up toward your scalp.
Hold… three… two… one… and release. Let your forehead become smooth and wide again.
Next, your eyes. Squeeze them tight, as if facing a dazzling sun, wrinkling your nose. Hold… three… two… one…
And release. Let your eyelids rest, barely closed. The area around your eyes softens.
Finally, your jaw. Gently clench your teeth, at half strength, and pull the corners of your mouth back. Feel the tension in your cheeks, in front of your ears, under your chin.
Hold… breathing through your nose… three… two… one…
And release. Your teeth part. Your lips may open slightly. Your tongue rests in your mouth.
[pause 3s]

If your mind has wandered during all this, to your day or to what's coming next, that's completely normal. The next contraction will bring you back into your body. That's one of the nice things about this method.
Feel your whole face, as if after a long sigh. Softer, heavier. No expression to hold for anyone.
Now your belly and back. Tighten your stomach muscles, as if bracing for a ball to land on your belly. Your stomach becomes firm and flat.
At the same time, if it's comfortable, draw your shoulder blades slightly toward each other, lifting your chest a little. Without arching hard, staying at half strength.
Feel your whole torso brace, front and back. Breathe as best you can, in small sips. Four… three… two… one…
And release everything. Your belly softens. Your back settles against the chair, or the floor.
Let your breath find its place in your belly again. It rises, it falls. More freely than before, maybe.
Notice how it feels to have your whole torso relaxed, your pelvis sinking into the chair or the floor.
[pause 3s]
Now your legs and feet. First your thighs: press your heels into the floor, and tighten your thighs and your glutes. Feel your legs become as hard as wood.
Hold… breathe… five… four… three… two… one…
And release. Your thighs spread out, your glutes soften, your legs grow heavy. Maybe you can feel warmth spreading from your hips down to your knees.
And finally, your feet and calves. Pull your toes up toward your face, flexing your ankles. Feel the stretch along the back of your calves, the tension down the front of your shins.
Go gently. If a cramp starts, let go right away.
Hold a little longer… three… two… one…
And release. Your feet drop, your toes spread, your ankles relax.
[pause 3s]
Now there's nothing left to tense. Your whole body can rest.
Do a quick sweep, from the bottom up. Feet, relaxed. Legs, heavy. Belly, soft. Back, resting. Hands, open. Shoulders, low. Face, smooth.

Now imagine a wave of relaxation starting at your feet and slowly rising. It moves through your calves, your knees, your thighs. It flows through your pelvis and your belly, and up along your back. It runs down your arms to your fingertips, then rises into your neck and spreads across your face.
If any area is still tight, tense it gently one last time, then let it go with an out-breath.
[pause 3s]
Think back to the area you noticed at the start. How does it feel now? Looser, or still a bit tight? Both are normal. You've learned something about it.
Savor the contrast. A few minutes ago, your muscles were on alert. Now they're allowed to do nothing at all. What you're feeling right now is what relaxation feels like, in your own body.
The more you practice, the faster you'll recognize this feeling. And the more easily you'll find it again, even in a few seconds, in the middle of a busy day.
Stay a little longer in this pleasant heaviness. Nothing to do, nothing to get right. Just the weight of your body, the warmth in your hands, your breath coming and going by itself.
Gently deepen your breathing. Move your fingers and toes. Stretch, if your body feels like it, as if you were waking up.
Open your eyes, taking your time.
Tonight, or tomorrow, if you catch yourself tense and unsure how to let go, remember the trick: squeeze a little… then release.

sessions.title: Full body scan
script: Welcome to this body scan. For the next ten minutes, you're simply going to visit your body, one area at a time, from your toes to the top of your head.
Choose your position. Lying on your back, arms by your sides, legs uncrossed. Or sitting, with your back upright and supported, feet flat on the floor, hands resting on your thighs.
Take a few seconds to adjust whatever needs adjusting. A cushion under your knees, a shoulder to shift, a waistband to loosen.
[pause 3s]
If you'd like, close your eyes. Otherwise, let your gaze rest on a spot on the floor or the ceiling, without staring.
Take a breath that's a little fuller than the others… and let it go.
Then another, feeling your body lean a little more into whatever is holding it. Your back, your pelvis, your heels settling down.

Before we begin, an intention. In a body scan, we're not trying to relax at all costs, or to change anything. We observe. We notice what's here, like a curious explorer taking in a landscape without judging it.
You may feel warmth, coolness, pressure, tingling, an itch, heaviness. Or nothing at all. Feeling nothing is an observation too. Whatever you notice is just right.
And if your mind wanders off, as it almost certainly will, notice that, without scolding yourself, and come back to whichever part of the body we've reached.
If some part of your body is painful, you can observe it from a distance, gently, or move straight on to the next area. You decide how close to get.
[pause 3s]
Now let your breathing find its own rhythm. It doesn't need to be slow or deep. It's just as it is.
Simply notice where you feel it most clearly. Maybe at your nostrils, maybe in your chest, maybe in your belly. This breath will keep you company for the whole journey.

Bring your attention down to your feet. First your toes. The big toe, then the others, all the way to the little one. Can you feel them without moving them? Maybe they're touching each other. Maybe you can feel the fabric of your socks, or the air on your skin.

Then the soles of your feet. The padded part beneath your toes, the arch, the heel. If you're sitting, notice the pressure of the floor. If you're lying down, the weight of your heels on the mattress or the mat.
The tops of your feet now, with their fine tendons just under the skin. And your ankles, with their small round bones on either side.
Imagine breathing all the way down into your feet. As you breathe in, your attention travels down to them. As you breathe out, they settle a little more, heavy and still.
[pause 3s]
Your attention moves up into your legs. Your calves at the back, often a little denser. Your shins at the front, right under the skin.
Your knees. The front, the kneecap. The sides. And the soft hollow behind each knee, a place we often forget about. It may feel a little warmer, a little softer than the rest.
Let your knees release, as if they no longer had to hold your legs together. The joints can open ever so slightly with each out-breath.
Then your thighs, the biggest muscles in your body. Feel their weight. The backs of your thighs against the chair or the floor. Maybe the temperature under the fabric of your clothes.
Take a moment to compare your left leg and your right leg. Does one seem heavier, warmer, more present than the other? There's no right answer. It's just a way of sharpening your attention.
Simply observe. If you notice some tension, you can breathe with it, without demanding that it leave. Breathe in as you look at it, breathe out as you give it a little more room.
[pause 3s]
Now your pelvis. Your hips, on each side. Your seat, carrying much of your weight. Feel the points of contact, maybe one side pressing down a little more than the other.
Your pelvis is like a bowl that gathers the weight of your upper body. Let it grow heavy, widen, and rest completely on whatever is holding it.

Your belly, now. Notice how it moves with the breath: rising slightly, falling again. Notice too whether it feels tight or relaxed, warm or neutral, whether it's gurgling a little. All of that is part of the landscape.
The belly is often one of the first places stress settles. You don't have to force it to relax. Simply looking at it kindly already gives it a little room.
Then your lower back. The area that holds up your posture all day long. Feel the area around your kidneys, the muscles on either side of your spine.
Maybe stiffness, tiredness, warmth. Or a pleasant sense of rest. You don't need to do anything with what you find. You notice it, that's all.
[pause 3s]
Moving up to your chest. Feel your ribcage open a little as you breathe in, and close as you breathe out. Your ribs spreading apart, then drawing together.

If you can sense it, notice your heartbeat. No need to go looking for it. If it's there, it's there. This heart has been beating for you all along, day and night, without you ever having to think about it.
Then your upper back. The space between your shoulder blades, and the shoulder blades themselves. Feel them against the back of the chair or the floor.
And your shoulders. Notice where they are. High, low, rolled forward? No correcting, just noting. If they decide on their own to drop a little, let them.

Imagine each in-breath gently filling the space between your shoulder blades, and each out-breath letting your shoulders slide down, a little heavier, a little wider. A lot of tension quietly builds up here. You're giving it a moment's rest.
[pause 3s]
If you feel drowsiness creeping in, that's common when the body settles. You can open your eyes slightly, or take a fuller breath, to stay present.
Your attention now travels down both arms at once. Your upper arms. Your elbows, with their bony points. Your forearms, the skin a little thinner on the inside.
Your wrists. Then your hands. The backs of your hands, your palms. Each finger, from thumb to little finger. Your fingertips, often very sensitive. Maybe a pulse, a buzzing, some warmth.
Let your hands become completely idle. All day long they hold, type, and carry. For now, they have nothing to do.
[pause 3s]
Move up to your neck. The front, your throat, where the air passes through. The sides. And the back of your neck, which has been holding up your head since this morning.
Your face, now. Your jaw: notice whether your teeth are touching or not. Your mouth, your lips. Your tongue, resting in your mouth.
If your teeth are touching, let a small gap open between them. Your jaw can grow heavy, as if sinking gently toward your throat. Feel the ease spreading in front of your ears, across your temples.
Your cheeks. Your nose, and the air moving through your nostrils, a little cooler on the in-breath, a little warmer on the out-breath.
Your eyes, beneath your eyelids. The tiny muscles around your eyes, which work so hard in front of screens. Your eyebrows. Your forehead, broad and flat.
Let your forehead widen and smooth out, like a sheet of paper unfolded flat on a table.
Then the sides of your head, your ears. The back of your skull, resting or balanced. And finally, the top of your head. Maybe a light sensation, tingling, air, or nothing in particular.
[pause 3s]
Now widen your attention to take in your whole body at once. From your toes to the top of your head. As if you were stepping back to look at the whole landscape you've just travelled through.
One body, breathing. With its tense areas, its calm areas, its neutral areas. Everything welcomed in the same way.
Feel the breath move through this whole body. On the in-breath, like a wave rising from your feet to your head. On the out-breath, flowing back down to your toes.
[pause 3s]
Notice how this body feels now, compared to the start of the session. Not to judge whether it's better or worse. Just to see.
You've taken ten minutes to listen to it, without asking anything of it. That's a rare thing in a day.
Gently, let's come back. Let your breathing become a little fuller. Feel the weight of your body again, the points of contact with the floor or the chair.
Slowly move your fingers and toes. If you feel like it, stretch your arms, gently roll your head.
Become aware of the sounds around you. The room, the street, the silence.
When the moment feels right for you, open your eyes.

Throughout the day, you can keep a thread of this attention. When you stand up, walk, or sit down, simply notice one sensation, any sensation. It's a way of coming back to your body in just a few seconds.

sessions.title: Stress-relief yoga nidra
script: Welcome to this yoga nidra. It's a pause for deep recovery, like a nap, except that part of you stays listening. In a quarter of an hour, you'll get up rested and ready to pick up your day again.

This format is sometimes called non-sleep deep rest. Your body settles almost as it would in sleep, while a small part of you stays awake and listens. It's the nap you can't always take, offered to yourself in another way.
Lie down on your back, on a mat, a bed, or a sofa. Legs stretched out and slightly apart, arms a little away from your body, palms facing up if that's comfortable.
If your lower back pulls, slide a cushion under your knees. If you tend to get cold, cover yourself with a blanket: the body cools down as it rests.
[pause 3s]
Make any last adjustments. Move your shoulders, your head, your pelvis a little, until you find a position you could stay in for a long time without moving.
Then close your eyes. From now on, the idea is to stay as still as you can. If you need to move, do it slowly, then come back to rest.

The only instruction in yoga nidra is to keep listening to my voice. No need to concentrate hard. Let the words come to you. If you drift off for a moment, that's fine, you'll pick up the thread again further on.
Take a big breath in through your nose… and breathe out through your mouth, in a long sigh.
Once more. Breathe in… and let the whole weight of your body sink into the floor.
[pause 3s]
Become aware of the sounds around you. The most distant ones first. A car, voices, the wind, perhaps. Let your listening reach far, beyond the walls, without looking for anything in particular.
Then the closer sounds, in the room. A humming fridge, a ticking clock, the faint rustle of your clothes. And finally, the sound of your own breathing, very close.
Let them all be there, without holding on to any of them. They pass by, like clouds. No sound is a disturbance: each one simply becomes part of the background.
Now feel your body lying down. The points of contact with the floor: the back of your head, your shoulder blades, your elbows, the backs of your hands, your pelvis, your calves, your heels.
Feel the weight of each of these points. The floor holds you completely. There's nothing to hold back, nothing to hold up.
Say to yourself, silently: I am lying down, I am resting, I am listening.
[pause 3s]
Now comes the moment for your sankalpa. It's an intention: a short, positive phrase, said in the present tense, as if it were already true.
You may already have one. If not, here are a few for inspiration. I am calm and present. I am allowed to rest. I move through my days with more ease.
Choose one, or let your own appear. Don't look for the perfect phrase. Take the first one that feels right.
Now repeat it silently, slowly, with all your sincerity. A first time…
[pause 2s]
A second time, feeling it resonate a little more deeply…
[pause 2s]
And a third time, like a seed you place in soft earth.
[pause 2s]
Let your sankalpa settle. We'll come back to it at the end.

Now we're going to move your awareness around the body. I'll name a part of the body. When you hear it, simply rest your attention there for a second, then follow my voice to the next. Without moving.
Right side. The right thumb. Index finger. Middle finger. Ring finger. Little finger.
The palm of the right hand. The back of the hand. The wrist. The forearm. The elbow. The upper arm. The right shoulder. The armpit.
The right side of the chest. The waist, on the right. The right hip. The right thigh. The knee. The calf. The ankle.
The right heel. The sole of the foot. The top of the foot. The big toe. The second toe. The third. The fourth. The fifth.
The whole right side, from fingertips to toes. Present, heavy, at rest.
Left side. The left thumb. Index finger. Middle finger. Ring finger. Little finger.
The palm of the left hand. The back of the hand. The wrist. The forearm. The elbow. The upper arm. The left shoulder. The armpit.
The left side of the chest. The waist, on the left. The left hip. The left thigh. The knee. The calf. The ankle.
The left heel. The sole of the foot. The top of the foot. The big toe. The second toe. The third. The fourth. The fifth.
The whole left side, from fingertips to toes. Present, heavy, at rest.
The back of the body. Both heels. Both calves. The backs of the knees. The backs of the thighs. The buttocks.
The lower back. The middle of the back. The right shoulder blade. The left shoulder blade. The whole spine. The back of the neck. The back of the head.
The whole back of the body, resting on the floor, like a print left in wet sand.
The face. The crown of the head. The forehead. The right temple. The left temple. The right eyebrow. The left eyebrow. The space between the eyebrows.
The right eyelid. The left eyelid. The right eye. The left eye. The right ear. The left ear.
The nose. The right nostril. The left nostril. The right cheek. The left cheek. The upper lip. The lower lip. The place where the lips meet. The chin. The jaw. The throat.
The front of the body. The right collarbone. The left collarbone. The center of the chest. The upper belly. The navel. The lower belly.
The whole front of the body, rising gently with the breath.
Now the larger parts. The whole right leg. The whole left leg. Both legs together.
The whole right arm. The whole left arm. Both arms together.
The whole back. The whole front of the body. The whole head. The whole body, together. The whole body, lying down, at rest.
Feel your body as one single presence, from feet to head. Feel the space it takes up in the room, its shape, its outline, completely still.
Now become aware of your natural breathing. Don't change it. Watch it the way you'd watch waves from the shore, asking nothing of them.
Feel the air come in through your nostrils, a little cooler. And go out, a little warmer.
Feel your belly rising and falling, all on its own.
Each in-breath brings a little freshness. Each out-breath invites you to settle a little more deeply.

Now follow the path of the breath. It comes in through the nostrils, down through the throat, gently fills the chest, then the belly. And it travels back the other way: belly, chest, throat, nostrils. A quiet round trip, again and again.
We're going to count the breaths backward, from eleven down to one. Silently, without changing the breath. I'll start with you, and then you'll carry on alone.
Breathe in, and say to yourself: eleven. Breathe out, and say: eleven.
Breathe in: ten. Breathe out: ten.
Breathe in: nine. Breathe out: nine.
Breathe in: eight. Breathe out: eight.

Carry on like this, at your own pace, down to one. If you lose count, which happens a lot, simply start again at eleven. There's nothing to get right. The counting is just a thread to help you stay present.
Seven… six… each number a little calmer than the last… each out-breath a little longer, a little softer.
[pause 5s]
Five… four… three… your body heavier and heavier, your mind quieter and quieter.
Two… one.
Let go of the counting, wherever you've got to. Come back to the breath, simple and easy. Let the body breathe in its own way.
[pause 3s]
Now we'll explore opposite sensations. Let them arise from memory, without forcing. If they don't really come, simply imagine them.

Awaken the feeling of heaviness. Your body is becoming heavy. Legs heavy, as if filled with sand. Arms heavy, resting. Head heavy, sinking into the pillow. Your whole body weighs down, as it does after a long day of walking.
Eyelids heavy. Shoulders heavy. Your back sinking into the floor, as if into warm sand. Everything is heavy, and everything is held.
And now, lightness. Your body is becoming light, very light. Like a cork floating on water. Arms light, legs light. As if the floor were barely holding you anymore.
Hands so light they could float away. Chest light, like a feather carried by the breath. Your whole body drifting, barely touching down.
Heaviness… and lightness. Let the two sensations come in turn, without preferring one. Heavy as a stone… light as a soap bubble.
Now awaken the feeling of warmth. Remember your hands around a mug of hot chocolate in winter. Or the sun on your skin, late on a summer afternoon. Warmth spreading through your whole body.
It starts in your belly, glows through your chest, flows down your arms to your hands, slips down your legs to your feet. A soft, enveloping warmth.
And now, coolness. Your feet in a river in springtime. The crisp air of a February morning on your face as you step outside. Your whole body becoming cool.
A clean coolness on your cheeks, your forehead, the backs of your hands. Like slipping between cool sheets on a summer night.
Warmth… and coolness. Your body knows how to move from one to the other. Now rest in a temperature that feels just right.

One last pair, closer to your everyday life. Remember a hectic moment, without choosing the worst one. A packed train platform, a phone that won't stop ringing, a morning where everything piles up. Just notice, for a moment, how your body remembers it. Maybe a shoulder creeping up, a breath growing shorter.

And now, let that image drift away. Remember a moment of calm. A Sunday morning with no alarm, a bench in the sun, the quiet of a house where everyone is still asleep. Let that calm settle into your body, and fill all the space.
Notice that your body knows how to do both. It knows how to rev up, and it knows how to come back to calm. For now, it's resting in the calm.
[pause 3s]
Now I'll name some images, one after another. Let each one appear however it comes, blurry or sharp, then let it go. If an image doesn't speak to you, simply wait for the next.
An open window, on a summer morning. The curtain barely moving.
White sheets drying in the wind, in a garden.
A lighthouse at the end of a jetty, in Brittany. Waves breaking softly on the rocks.
A cup of tea steaming on a wooden table.
A field of lavender in the sun, the hum of bees.
Footprints in fresh snow, the soft crunch under your shoes.
A rowing boat, still, on a lake as smooth as a mirror.
A cat curled up on an armchair, purring.
Rain on a roof, at night, steady and gentle.
Warm bread coming out of the oven, its smell filling the kitchen.
A cobbled street shining after a shower.
An empty beach in winter, the wet sand reflecting the sky.
A fire in the hearth, the embers glowing.
A mountain path at sunrise.
A pine forest, the smell of resin, light falling between the branches.
The sky, just before the stars appear.
[pause 4s]
Now let all the images fade. Rest in the calm, dark space behind your eyelids. Nothing to look at, nothing to do. Just being here.
This space is wide, quiet, without edges. You can rest here as long as you like. All that's here is the breath, and this peaceful presence.
[pause 4s]
Now return to your sankalpa, the intention you chose at the beginning. The same phrase, with the same words.

Repeat it three times, silently, with sincerity. Feel it settle inside you, somewhere deep and calm. It will keep making its way, quietly, even when you're no longer thinking about it. No effort, no pressure. Like a friend gently reminding you of what matters to you.
[pause 5s]
This yoga nidra is coming to an end. We're going to come back gradually.
If you dozed off at times, or don't remember everything, that's perfectly fine. Your body still benefited from the rest, even when your attention wandered away.
Become aware of your breathing. Let it deepen a little, become more present.
Feel your body lying down again, its weight, its points of contact with the floor.
Become aware of the room you're in. The temperature of the air. The light, perhaps, through your eyelids. The sounds around you.
Remind yourself what day it is, what time of day, what you're going to do next.
Let your attention widen, little by little, from your body to the room, from the room to the rest of your day.
Start to move gently. Fingers, toes. Slowly circle your wrists, your ankles.
If it feels good, stretch out full length, arms above your head, like a cat after a nap. Yawn if you feel like it.
Then roll gently onto your side. Stay there for a moment, eyes still closed.
[pause 3s]
When the moment feels right for you, use your hands to sit up. Open your eyes, slowly. Let the light come back in.
Take one last full breath, feeling the energy returning to your body.
You've given your body a real chance to recover. Take this calm with you, and return to your day refreshed and rested, at your own pace.
This practice is now complete.

sessions.title: Deep body scan
script: Hello, and welcome to this deep body scan. You've chosen to take twenty-five minutes just for yourself. A Sunday, a day off, a quiet late afternoon… Whenever it is, this time belongs to you.
To begin, find a place where you won't be disturbed. If you can, switch your phone to "do not disturb", so nothing interrupts the session.

Lie down on your back, on a mat, a blanket, or your bed. Legs stretched out and slightly apart, feet falling naturally out to the sides. Arms by your sides, a little away from your body, palms facing up or down, whichever you prefer.

If this position isn't comfortable for you, you can bend your knees, slide a cushion under your legs, or do the whole practice sitting in an armchair. What matters is that your body feels well supported.
A blanket can help: when we stay still, we often cool down a little.
[pause 3s]
Close your eyes, if that feels good. Or keep them half-open, your gaze resting low, not fixed on anything.

Before going further, an intention. This scan isn't about reaching a particular state. Not perfect relaxation, not an empty mind. It's about introducing yourself to your body, just as it is right now, moment by moment, with curiosity and gentleness.

You'll probably notice sensations that are pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral. They all have their place. And you'll also notice your mind wandering, sometimes often. That's what minds do. Each time you realize it, you can simply come back, without judging yourself. That coming back is the practice itself.

This approach comes from mindfulness-based stress reduction programs, developed more than forty years ago. There, the body scan is practiced slowly and regularly, as a way of learning to inhabit the body rather than rushing through it without noticing.
If you fall asleep, that's not a failure either. Maybe your body needed the rest. But the invitation is to stay awake, attentive to what's here, for as long as you can.
And if any part of your body is painful or injured, you're always free to choose your distance. You can observe it from afar, very gently, or simply move on to the next area.
[pause 3s]
Start by feeling your body as a whole. Its shape, its length, its mass resting on the floor.
Feel all the places where it touches whatever is holding it. The back of your head. Your shoulders. Your back. Your pelvis. The backs of your legs. Your heels.
Notice where the pressure is strongest, and where it's lighter. Notice too the places that don't touch: the hollow of your neck, the curve of your lower back, the backs of your knees.
With each out-breath, allow your body to give itself a little more fully to this support. You don't have to hold it up. The floor takes care of that.
Feel the surface beneath you. Its texture, its firmness, maybe its temperature. It holds you completely, effortlessly, asking nothing in return.
[pause 3s]
Now bring your attention to your breathing. Without changing it. Simply notice where you feel it most clearly today. Maybe at the nostrils, maybe in the chest, maybe in the belly.
Let your attention rest on the movement of your belly. It rises gently as you breathe in. It falls as you breathe out.
Feel the moment the in-breath begins. The moment it ends. The small pause, sometimes, before the out-breath comes. And the small pause at the end of the out-breath, before it all begins again.
You've been breathing since this morning without thinking about it. Now this breath will keep you company for the whole journey. Every time you get lost, it will be there to bring you back.
Stay with it for a few more breaths. Breathe in, the belly rises. Breathe out, it falls. Nothing more to do.
[pause 3s]

In this scan, we'll use the breath in a particular way. When we arrive at an area of the body, you can imagine breathing into that area. The air coming in through your nose, traveling down through the body to reach it, then rising back up and out.
It's not a physical exercise, of course. It's a way of directing your attention, making your presence more alive, more gentle. If it feels strange, simply observe the area while you breathe normally.
Now let your attention travel down the whole length of your body to your left foot. As if you were moving a beam of light from your head down to your toes.
Pause at your left big toe. Feel it. Maybe it's touching the toe next to it. Maybe you can feel the sheet or your sock, the temperature of the air.
Then the second toe. The third, the fourth. And the little toe, right at the edge.

Some toes may be hard to tell apart. You don't need to move them to feel them. If you don't feel anything in particular, simply notice that "nothing". It's a neutral sensation, and it's just as interesting.
Notice the spaces between your toes, too. Skin touching skin, or air passing between them. Tiny sensations we almost never notice.
[pause 3s]

Now the sole of your left foot. Start with the padded part just beneath your toes. Then the arch, that hollow which hardly ever touches the ground. And the heel, firmer, carrying the weight of the resting foot.
Notice the sensations, the subtlest ones you can find. Pressure. A faint tingling. Warmth or coolness. A pulse, perhaps, if you stay attentive for a while.
Think of everything this foot has carried today, and every other day. The stairs, the pavements, the hours standing. For now, it has nothing left to carry.
The top of your left foot now. The thinner skin, the tendons just beneath. The sides of the foot. And the ankle, with its two small rounded bones, on the inside and the outside.
Feel your left foot as a whole.

And for the first time, try breathing into this foot. Breathe in, imagining the air traveling all the way down your leg to your toes. Breathe out, imagining the air rising from your foot back up to your nostrils.
Once more. Breathe in… the breath travels down, to the heel, to the tips of the toes. Breathe out… it rises again, and your foot settles a little more.
[pause 3s]
Then, on your next out-breath, let this foot fade from your attention. It's still there, of course. But you let it rest, and you carry on.
Your attention moves up into your lower left leg. The calf at the back, resting on the floor, with its weight, its density. The shin at the front, the bone just under the skin.
Notice whether your calf is tense or relaxed. Whether one area is more present than another. Nothing to correct. Only to discover.
Breathe into your calf. As you breathe in, you notice it. As you breathe out, you let it become a little heavier, a little softer, like warm clay.
Your left knee. The kneecap at the front. The sides of the knee. And the soft hollow just behind it, a gentle place we often forget.

If this knee carries pain, or an old injury, you can approach it with care. Stay at the edge of the sensation, without diving in. Breathe around it. If it's too much, simply move on. You're always free to choose your distance.
[pause 3s]
Now your left thigh. A large space. The front of the thigh, the inside, the outside. The back, resting on the floor. Feel the volume of this muscle, its heaviness.
It's one of the most powerful muscles in your body. It lifts you out of your chair, carries you up the stairs, holds you up. For once, let it rest completely.
Then your left hip, where the leg meets the pelvis. A deep joint, nestled inside the body. Maybe you can barely feel it. That's fine too.
And now become aware of your whole left leg, from the toes to the hip. One area, one presence.
Breathe into this whole leg. Breathe in, the air travels down to the tips of your toes. Breathe out, it rises again, perhaps carrying a little tiredness away with it.
Notice whether your left leg feels different from your right one now. Heavier, warmer, more alive… or not at all. Just observe.
[pause 3s]
Then let your left leg rest, and move your attention over to your right foot. Take your time making this journey.
Your right big toe. The second toe. The third, the fourth, the little toe.
Here too, welcome whatever is present. Maybe this foot seems easier to feel than the other, or harder. Each side has its own story.
The sole of your right foot. The part beneath the toes, the arch, the heel. Notice the weight of the heel, its contact with the floor, the small area of pressure that carries the whole foot.
If your mind has wandered off, to a memory, a plan, something to do tomorrow… notice where it went. And, without scolding yourself, walk it back to this foot. As many times as you need.
[pause 3s]
The top of your right foot, the thin skin, the tendons. Your right ankle, its rounded bones on either side. Your whole right foot.
Breathe into this foot. The in-breath travels down to it. The out-breath leaves from it. And with every breath, it becomes a little heavier, a little more still.
Then let it rest, and move up to your right calf. Feel its weight on the floor, its rounded shape, maybe a little tension near the Achilles tendon. Then the shin, at the front.
Your right knee. The kneecap, the sides, the hollow just behind. Take time to pause on each one.
Breathe into your right calf, your right knee. Let them grow a little heavier with every out-breath.
Notice the quality of the sensations, rather than their names. Is it fixed, or does it change from one moment to the next? Is it in one spot, or spread out?
[pause 3s]

Your right thigh. The front, the sides, the back pressing into the floor. Maybe you can feel the boundary between your skin and the fabric of your clothes, or the warmth building where your leg touches the floor. Your right hip, deep inside, where the leg joins the pelvis.

Then your whole right leg, from the toes to the hip. Breathe into this leg. Breathe in, all the way to the tips of your toes. Breathe out, all the way back to your nostrils. Once more, at your own pace.
Now widen your attention to include both legs at once. Both feet, both calves, both knees, both thighs. Two long presences, resting, with nothing to do for once.
Feel them heavy, held, maybe a little warmer than at the start. Let them sink into the floor, as if leaving their print in wet sand.
[pause 3s]

If, at this point, your body wants to move, scratch, or change position, that's normal. You can first observe the urge itself for a few seconds, with curiosity. Then, if you choose to move, do it slowly, feeling each stage of the movement. And come back to stillness.

We arrive at the pelvis. Let your legs rest, and bring your attention to the whole pelvic area. The hips, on either side. The buttocks, carrying your weight on the floor. The bones of the pelvis, like a large bowl.
Notice the areas of contact and pressure. Maybe one side pressing down more. Maybe some warmth, some heaviness.
The lower belly, inside the pelvis. The organs, the skin, the pelvic floor muscles at the very bottom, which can soften too.
The pelvis is the body's center of gravity. When it settles, the rest often follows. Feel it heavy, stable, well grounded.
Breathe into the whole pelvis. Imagine the breath filling it like a bowl filling with warm water, then slowly emptying.
[pause 3s]
Then the belly. Feel it moving with the breath. The skin stretching slightly as you breathe in. The belly falling back as you breathe out.

Notice whether it's soft or tight. The belly is often a place where we hold a lot without realizing it. If you feel some tightness, breathe gently toward it. You don't have to chase it away. Let it be there, surrounded by your breath.
Notice the more internal sensations too: a gurgle, a feeling of hunger or fullness, a slight movement. All of that is part of you.
The upper belly, just below the ribs. The navel, at the center. The sides of your waist, widening a little as the air comes in. Let this whole space become soft and open.
[pause 3s]
Now your lower back. The area around the kidneys, just above the pelvis. Notice whether it touches the floor, or whether there's a small hollow. The muscles on either side of the spine.
This area works hard during our sitting days. Breathe into your lower back. Imagine that with each in-breath, it widens a little. With each out-breath, it sinks a little further into the floor.
Then the middle of your back, behind the stomach. And the upper back, up to the shoulder blades. Feel the spine connecting all of it, like a central axis from the base of your back to your neck.
Maybe some areas of your back feel very present, and others almost silent. The silent areas, the ones you can't feel, deserve your attention too. They're part of you just the same.
Let your whole back settle, vertebra by vertebra, like a ribbon slowly unrolled along the floor.
[pause 3s]
Now the chest. Feel the whole ribcage, with its ribs at the front, the sides, the back. It widens in every direction as you breathe in. It narrows as you breathe out.
The breastbone, in the center. The collarbones, at the top. The muscles between the ribs, working gently with every breath.

And in the center of your chest, slightly to the left, your heart. Maybe you can feel it beating. Or maybe not, and that's completely normal. You can simply know it's there, beating since your very first day, never asking for a break.
If it feels good, rest your attention on this area with a little gratitude. This heart, these lungs, are working for you right now.
Breathe into your chest. Let the breath fill this space, without forcing, and leave it, without holding on.

Feel the space between your breastbone at the front and your shoulder blades at the back. A space that gently expands as the air comes in, and rests as it leaves. Let your chest open, effortlessly, like a window eased open on a summer morning.
[pause 3s]
Now your shoulders. Left shoulder, right shoulder. Their roundness, their contact with the floor. Notice whether they've crept up toward your ears, or rolled a little forward.

A lot settles into the shoulders: responsibilities, effort, hours in front of a screen. You don't need to analyze. Simply breathe into your shoulders. And if, as you breathe out, they want to drop a little, to widen, let them.
Imagine them slowly melting toward the floor, like snow under a March sun. Your upper back widens, your neck lengthens.
Let your attention slide from your shoulders down both arms at once. The upper arms, down to the elbows. Feel their weight on the floor. The elbows, their bony points, the softer inner side.
The forearms. Notice the difference between the side touching the floor and the side open to the air. Maybe a little warmer on one side, a little cooler on the other.
The wrists. Then the hands. The palms. The backs of the hands. The fingers: both thumbs, both index fingers, both middle fingers, both ring fingers, both little fingers.
The fingertips. One of the most sensitive areas of the body. Stay here a moment. Maybe a tingling, a pulse, a faint warmth. Maybe you can feel the air on your skin, or the touch of fabric.
Breathe into your hands. Imagine the air reaching your palms and filling them with a gentle warmth. Your hands, which do so much all day, can stay open and empty.
[pause 3s]
Now breathe into both arms, all the way. Breathe in, from your nostrils to your fingertips. Breathe out, from your fingertips back to your nostrils.
Notice whether your left and right arms feel the same, or whether each has its own character today. The one that writes, carries, holds the phone may feel a little more present, a little more tired.
And let your arms rest, heavy and still. Hands open, with nothing to grasp, nothing to hold on to.
Moving up to the neck. The front of the neck, the throat, where air and voice pass through. Notice whether your throat feels tight or open. Maybe you can even notice the movement of swallowing.
Let your throat open and widen, as at the very beginning of a yawn.
The sides of the neck. The back of the neck, which carries your head all day long, and can finally hand it over to the floor.
Breathe into the back of your neck. With each out-breath, imagine it lengthening a little, the space between your head and shoulders gently growing.
[pause 3s]
Now come to your face, taking your time. The jaw. Notice where your teeth are. Are they touching? Let them part, if they want to. The cheek muscles, just in front of your ears.
The mouth. The lips, the upper lip, the lower lip, the place where they meet. The tongue, resting inside. The roof of your mouth, your gums.

Breathe into your jaw. With each out-breath, imagine it growing heavier, sliding gently downward. Many people clench their teeth without knowing it, at night or in front of a screen. Here, it can finally rest.
The nose. Feel the air coming in through your nostrils, cool. The air going out, a little warmer. A tiny sensation, renewed with every breath.

The cheeks. The eyes, beneath the eyelids. Notice whether they're moving, or resting. The area around the eyes, the small muscles that tighten when we stare at a screen. The eyebrows, and the space between them.
Let your eyes sink gently back into their sockets, as if resting on a velvet cushion. Nothing to look at, nothing to watch over.
[pause 3s]
The forehead. Wide, from the line of your eyebrows to your hairline. Notice whether it's furrowed or smooth. The temperature of the skin.
Imagine a cool hand resting on your forehead, gently smoothing it from one eyebrow to the other.
The temples. The ears, and whatever they're hearing right now. The back of your skull, resting heavily on the floor or the cushion.
And finally, the top of your head. The scalp, maybe a faint tingling. The highest point of your body.
Breathe into your whole head and face. Breathe in, and let your face open a little to the air. Breathe out, and let it soften. No expression to keep up. No one to put on a face for.
[pause 3s]
Now widen your attention to the whole body at once. From your toes to the top of your head. Front, back, sides. The surface of the skin, and the inside.
One whole body, breathing. Feel it widen slightly as you breathe in, and settle as you breathe out.

Imagine your whole body breathing, as one single surface. As if every cell of your skin were gently taking part in the breath. Air coming in through the whole body. Air going out through the whole body.
There may still be tense areas, buzzing areas, neutral areas, areas that seem absent. Let them all exist together, in this wide space of your presence.

Feel your skin as an envelope that holds all of you, from the soles of your feet to the top of your head. Inside, your heart beating, your breath moving, warmth spreading. Everything working, without you having to step in.
Maybe the outline of your body becomes a little blurry, and you're no longer quite sure where your hands end and the floor begins. If so, let it be. If not, that's fine too.
[pause 4s]
Simply rest here, in the experience of this breathing body. If your attention wanders, come back to the breath, or to the weight of your body on the floor.
Breathe in… and feel your whole body welcoming the air. Breathe out… and feel your whole body settling, a little heavier, a little calmer.
There's nowhere to go, nothing to improve. Just this body, this breath, this moment.
[pause 4s]
Notice how you feel now. Not how you're supposed to feel. Just how it is. Take a moment to recognize that you gave yourself this time, and that your body was with you all the way.
You can come back to these twenty-five minutes whenever you like. They aren't lost. With practice, this awareness of the body becomes more and more familiar, even in the middle of your day.
Now we'll come back, very gently. There's no rush.
Start by deepening your breath a little. Let the in-breath grow fuller, more present. Feel the air filling your belly, your chest.
Become aware of the sounds around you. The room, the building, the street. The world carrying on, quietly, on the other side of your eyelids.
Feel the temperature of the air on your face. The light, perhaps, through your closed eyes.
[pause 3s]
Start to move, very slowly. Fingers and toes. Hands, feet. Make small circles with your wrists and ankles.
If you feel like it, stretch out full length. Arms above your head, legs long. The way you stretch on a morning with no alarm.
Then roll gently onto your side, and stay there for a few breaths, like a child waking from a nap.
When the moment feels right, use your hands to push yourself up to sitting. Your head comes up last.
Open your eyes, slowly. Let your gaze rest on what's around you, as if seeing it for the first time.

For the rest of your day, keep a thread of connection with your body. A hand around a warm mug, your feet on the pavement, the air on your face. A single sensation is enough to bring you back here, to the present, to your body.
